author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: When the Plan Changes
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
Danse had set out two mugs before I told him I couldn't stay.

He didn't say anything at first. He looked at the table, then at my face, then at the clock above the workshop door.

"I thought we had agreed on dinner."

"We did."

"You've made another commitment?"

"Yes. Greg needs help arranging supplies for a music night at Starwake. I told him I'd come over after the afternoon repairs."

Danse nodded once. His expression went blank in the way it did when he was trying to turn an emotional response into a procedure.

"I see."

I took off my coat, then put it back on. The movement felt ridiculous.

"I should have checked our schedule before saying yes," I admitted. "I'm sorry."

"Is this an emergency?"

"No."

He looked at me.

"Then why must our plans change?"

The question had an edge. Not an accusation, exactly. A real question from someone who had spent years living by orders and wasn't always certain how to ask for something without sounding as though he was issuing one.

"I don't know that they must," I said. "I want to keep both promises. I haven't worked out how."

He exhaled through his nose.

"Then we should work it out."

We stood there looking at the table.

It was such a small thing, two mugs and a meal we'd planned to share, but I knew how much the evening meant to him. Danse didn't need an elaborate dinner. He wanted the predictability of a time I'd chosen to spend with him, not a gap left over after every other obligation had been met.

"Can we sit?" I asked.

He pulled out a chair.

I did the same.

For a moment we sat in silence, listening to the ticking clock and the faint hum of the workshop furnace.

"I don't want you to feel as though you have to compete," I said.

Danse's shoulders tightened.

"I haven't said that."

"No. But I can see something is bothering you."

He looked down at his hands.

"I was under the impression that our arrangements were clear."

"They are. I'm ethically non-monogamous, and I prefer polyamory. You know I care about you, and that I also care about other people. But that doesn't excuse me for forgetting a plan."

He rubbed one thumb against the edge of the mug.

"I don't want to be the person who demands you cancel everything else."

"You're not."

"Sometimes I don't know where the line is."

"Between asking for reassurance and making a demand?"

He nodded.

I leaned forward.

"Tell me what you actually need."

Danse stared at the clock again, as though it might provide a regulation for this situation.

"I wanted a quiet evening," he said finally. "Not because I wanted to prevent you from seeing anyone else. Because I wanted to be with you without worrying that something would pull us apart in the middle of it."

I felt the familiar sting of realizing I'd hurt someone by treating their time as flexible simply because they were patient.

"That's fair."

He looked at me.

"Is it?"

"Yes."

"Then what do we do?"

I took out my notebook and checked the time. The supply meeting at Starwake was supposed to be a short one. Greg had asked for help with chairs and a sound check, but Mara and Pip were both already scheduled for the first hour. There was no reason I had to stay through the evening.

"I can go to the setup meeting, then come back for dinner at seven," I said. "If you're willing to eat later."

Danse considered that.

"I can."

"And if something changes, I'll send word before the time arrives."

He nodded.

Then he looked at me more directly.

"What if I'd said no?"

"To a later dinner?"

"Yes."

"Then we'd look for another time. Or I'd ask Greg whether somebody else could handle the setup. You don't have to accept every compromise just because I suggest it."

He sat back.

"I think I needed to hear that."

I smiled a little.

"Me too."

The conversation could have ended there. Instead, Danse cleared his throat.

"There's something else."

I waited.

"At the yard, people talk."

"About us?"

"About your other relationships. About where you go. They act as though knowing your schedule entitles them to an opinion of you."

My jaw tightened.

"What did they say?"

He hesitated.

"I don't want to repeat it. I told them our private lives weren't their business."

"Thank you."

He looked uncertain.

"Was that the right response?"

"It was yours. I appreciate it. And if somebody asks me, I'll speak for myself."

"I didn't want to make decisions for you."

"That's one of the reasons I love you."

The words escaped before I could measure them.

He went still.

Then his face softened.

"I love you too," he said.

I reached across the table. He took my hand.

We sat together for a few minutes longer, not solving every future argument but making the next one a little less frightening.

At Starwake, Greg was setting up a small stage with a volunteer crew. The railings had been repaired, and the weather was clear. I helped move the equipment list to a dry board and checked that the new storage space wasn't blocking the walkway.

Greg looked at me.

"You okay?"

"Yes. I need to leave at six."

He grinned.

"Look at you, having boundaries."

"Don't sound so proud."

"I'm impressed. It's rare around here."

We finished the inventory early. I left the rest to the volunteers who had agreed to handle it.

On the way back to Brasswatch, I stopped at Mara's bakery for bread. She handed me a warm loaf and a look that suggested she knew more about the square's gossip than I wanted to imagine.

"People love a story," she said.

"Even when they don't know the people in it."

"Especially then."

I carried the bread home.

Danse had cleared the worktable and set out the two mugs again. This time, when he saw me, he smiled.

"You're early."

"I know. Terrible habit."

He stood.

I put the bread down, went around the table, and kissed him before he could ask whether I had brought the correct fittings.

He was startled for half a second. Then he returned the kiss with a warmth that made the long day finally feel finished. His hand rested against my cheek, steady and careful.

"May I ask a question?" he murmured.

"Always."

"Will you stay tonight?"

"I'd like to."

He held my gaze.

"Because you want to?"

"Because I want to."

He nodded, satisfied.

We ate dinner after the furnace was banked. Later, we sat on the back steps and listened to the night settle over the yard. There were no new orders, no promises of perfect scheduling, and no need to make another person's absence into proof of anything.

Tomorrow I had other plans.

Tonight I was here.

Both were true.
